spotlight.title: Ration cards and wartime controls
spotlight.standfirst: Rationing came to India's cities in 1943: a card for each family, a daily grain allowance and queues for what was scarce.

items.title: A ration card for Bombay
items.summary: Rationing of foodgrains began in Bombay in 1943; the basic allowance was 16 ounces of grain a day, later cut to 12 ounces after a poor harvest, and every family in the city held a ration card, though villages were left out.

sources.label: International Labour Review, 1944: food rationing and wartime controls (ILO)

items.title: Who came first
items.summary: The Priority Classes Distribution Scheme favoured defence factory workers, soldiers and civil servants in industrial centres such as Calcutta, leaving rural people unprotected; statutory rationing in the big cities followed the Woodhead Commission of 1944-45 and became the base of the Public Distribution System.

sources.label: GKToday: War-time scarcity and colonial economy

items.title: Rice from Burma stops
items.summary: Rice imported from Burma, about 15 to 20 percent of what Bengal ate, was cut off after the fall of Rangoon in March 1942, while price caps, bans on moving grain between provinces and army stockpiling caused local scarcity, hoarding and black marketing.

sources.label: GKToday: War-time scarcity and colonial economy

items.title: Cloth and kerosene
items.summary: Industry was redirected to military goods, leaving a severe shortage of civilian goods such as cloth and kerosene.

sources.label: GKToday: War-time scarcity and colonial economy

items.title: Prices and the paper rupee
items.summary: Wartime spending was paid for by issuing paper currency against sterling securities held in London, and the price index of essential goods rose steeply from 1939 to 1945, hurting landless labourers, town wage-earners and fixed-income families.

sources.label: GKToday: War-time scarcity and colonial economy
